claims.text: Stone handicrafts are made by artisans from natural stones such as marble, sandstone, soapstone and granite.

quotes.quote: Stone handicrafts are traditional and decorative products crafted by artisans using natural stones such as marble, sandstone, soapstone, and granite.
Different types of stones like, marble, soapstone and sand stone are used by craftsmen in India.

claims.text: Stone handicrafts include sculptures, idols, vases, lamps, tabletops, jali panels, trays and wall hangings.

quotes.quote: These items often include sculptures, idols, vases, lamps, tabletops, jali panels, trays, wall hangings, and home décor elements.

claims.text: Stone carving is practised all over India, and the types of stone carved reflect regional variation in which stones are available.

quotes.quote: Stone carving is practised all over India but the types of stones used for carving reflect the regional variation in the availability of different stones.

claims.text: The Varanasi soft stone statement of case says stone working is no longer restricted to temple carving and deities but also makes panels, tiles, paper weights and pen stands.

quotes.quote: Of late stone working is not only restricted to ornate carvings on temples or sculptures ofdeities, but also used in making items like carved panels, tiles, paper weights, pen stands, models of historical buildings

claims.text: Uttar Pradesh's MSME department names Rajasthan as famous for marble carving and Odisha for soapstone idols.

quotes.quote: Some regions are famous for specific styles, like Rajasthan for marble carving or Odisha for soapstone idols.

claims.text: Mamallapuram is one of the stone carving centres of India, where hundreds of carvers mainly make sculptures of Hindu gods and goddesses.

quotes.quote: The town of Mamallapuram is one of the stone carving centres of India
Hundreds of carvers produce mainly sculptures of different Hindu gods and goddesses and their work is based on Hindu stone carving tradition.

claims.text: Kenoyer, Vidale and Bhan described Khambhat, at the time they wrote, as one of the largest stone bead working centres of the world, important for over 3000 years.

quotes.quote: At present the city of Khambhat (Cambay) is one of the largest stone bead working centres of the world, and it has been an important centre for over 3000 years of documented history.

claims.text: Possehl described Cambay, an English corruption of Khambhat, as a centre for lapidary craftsmanship whose products reached a market on four continents.

quotes.quote: This name is an English corruption of Khambhat. It is a center for lapidary craftsmanship, its products reaching a market on four continents.

claims.text: Agra has two stone craft traditions, carving and inlay, and stone carving, of ancient origin, is found in various centres of north India.

quotes.quote: The rich architectural heritage of Agra is enriched by two craft traditions, those of stone carving and inlay. Stone carving has ancient origins, and in fact is found in various centres of north India.

claims.text: In a 2010-2011 study, Dhakotha in Odisha had two soapstone crafts, Patthar Kundo turning and carving, with approximately 450 soapstone craftsmen active.

quotes.quote: under the political subdivision of Anandapur in Kendujhar district of Odisha

There are two different soapstone craft forms exist in Dhakotha, i.e., ପତ୍ଥର କୁଣ୍ଡ or Pather Kundo Craft and Soapstone Craving Craft; and there is a number of approximately 450 soapstone craftsmen are active.
This craft study cum design intervention initiative was conducted during 2010-2011 by this author.

claims.text: In Jha's 2010-2011 study, of approximately 500 soapstone craftsmen at Dhakotha, around 400 were in stone carving and approximately 50 in Pather Kundo stone turning.

quotes.quote: Out of approximately 500 soapstone craftsmen, around 400 craftsmen are involved in stone carving or statue making craft; while another pool of approximately 50 craftsmen are involved in traditional Pather Kundo or stone turning craft.
This craft study cum design intervention initiative was conducted during 2010-2011 by this author.

claims.text: Stone carvers from Puri, Bhubaneswar, Lalitagiri and Khiching in Odisha carve statues of deities and the Konark wheel, horse, elephant and lion.

quotes.quote: Stone Carvings of Odisha reflects a glorious cultural past and rich heritage.
The stone carvers from Puri, Bhubaneswar, Lalitagiri & Khiching are engaged in making beautiful stone statues include Krishna and Radha, Laxmi, Vishnu, Durga, Buddha and Ganesh
Surasundaris heavenly beauties playing on different musical instruments at Konark temple, the Konark wheel, horse, elephant, lion etc.

claims.text: Possehl wrote that beadmaking in the Cambay area of Gujarat seems to have started as early as the third millennium BC, with the Harappan settlement at Lothal.

quotes.quote: The craft seems to have started here as early as the third millennium B.C. with the founding of the Harappan settlement at Lothal
Cambay is a small city, population about 50,000, on the coast of Gujarat state in western India.

claims.text: Lothal, dated to about 2400 to 1700 BC, made beads on a large scale from chalcedony and other agates, jasper and rock crystal.

quotes.quote: This ancient town, which dates to ca. 2400-1700 B.C., had a large scale bead manufacturing operation taking a variety of raw materials -chalcedony and other agates, jasper, rock crystal and the like-and turning them into beads

claims.text: Beads made at Lothal were used by the Harappans themselves and shipped to places as distant as Mesopotamia.

quotes.quote: turning them into beads that were used by the Harappans themselves and shipped to places as distant as Mesopotamia.

claims.text: The stone bead industry of Pakistan and western India can be traced back to the Harappan phase of the Indus tradition, dated to around 2500 BC.

quotes.quote: With the aid of archaeological research, the stone bead industry in Pakistan and western India can be traced back even earlier to the cities and villages of the Harappan phase of the Indus tradition, dated to around 2500 BC.

claims.text: Harappan beads were chipped to a rough shape, ground smooth and then perforated with stone drills propelled by a bow.

quotes.quote: The first step involved a two-phase chipping process which formed the beads to their rough shape. The bead was then ground to a smooth outline. The perforation of the bead was done next.
It is quite certain that the stone drills used in penetrating Harappan beads were propelled by a bow.

claims.text: Possehl found the same sequence of steps and the same basic technology as the Harappans still used in Cambay.

quotes.quote: It is of considerable interest that this sequence of steps and the same basic technology are still used today in Cambay.

claims.text: Before electricity, Cambay beads were polished by hand, sewn with slurry into a skin bag rolled across a floor between two men.

quotes.quote: Prior to the use of electricity and more elaborate mechanical contrivances, the polishing was done by hand. That is, beads and slurry were sewn into a skin bag and this was 'rolled' across a floor between two men.

claims.text: UNESCO's summary says the Mahabalipuram sanctuaries were carved out of rock by the Pallava kings along the Coromandel coast in the 7th and 8th centuries.

quotes.quote: This group of sanctuaries, founded by the Pallava kings, was carved out of rock along the Coromandel coast in the 7th and 8th centuries.
Mahabalipuram (or Mamallapuram), located along southeastern India's Coromandel Coast, was a celebrated port city of the Pallavas.

claims.text: UNESCO's statement of value says the Pallava monuments at Mahabalipuram mark the high quality of craftsmanship in the region during the 6th century CE.

quotes.quote: These majestic edifices mark the high quality of craftsmanship in the region during 6th century CE.
The Pallava dynasty, which ruled this area between 6th and 9th centuries CE, created these majestic edifices.

claims.text: The rathas of Mahabalipuram, so called because they resemble processional temple chariots, are five monolithic temples each hewn out of a huge boulder.

quotes.quote: The monolithic temples are locally called "ratha" (chariot), as they resemble the processional chariots of a temple. These five monolithic temples are each hewn out of a huge boulder.

claims.text: The influence of the Mahabalipuram sculptures, soft and supple in their modelling, spread to Cambodia, Annam and Java.

quotes.quote: The influence of the sculptures of Mahabalipuram, characterized by the softness and suppleness of their modelling, spread afar to places such as Cambodia, Annam and Java.

claims.text: The 13th-century Sun Temple at Konark represents the chariot of Surya, the sun god, and UNESCO calls it a testimony to the 13th-century kingdom of Orissa.

quotes.quote: the temple at Konarak is a monumental representation of the sun god Surya's chariot
Built in the 13th century, it is one of India's most famous Brahman sanctuaries.
Konârak is an outstanding testimony to the 13th-century kingdom of Orissa.

claims.text: On the north and south sides of the Konark temple are 24 carved wheels, each about 3 m in diameter.

quotes.quote: On the north and south sides are 24 carved wheels, each about 3 m in diameter, as well as symbolic motifs referring to the cycle of the seasons and the months.

claims.text: UNESCO's summary says the Konark temple chariot is led by a team of six horses.

quotes.quote: its 24 wheels are decorated with symbolic designs and it is led by a team of six horses.

claims.text: UNESCO's statement of value says the Konark temple represents a chariot of the Sun God with twelve pairs of wheels drawn by seven horses.

quotes.quote: the temple represents a chariot of the Sun God, with twelve pairs of wheels drawn by seven horses evoking its movement across the heavens.

claims.text: Legends of the Konark temple say its construction mobilised 1,200 workers for 12 years under the architect Bisu Moharana.

quotes.quote: the temple has raised up those lovely legends which are affiliated everywhere with absolute works of art: its construction caused the mobilization of 1,200 workers for 12 years. The architect, Bisu Moharana, having left his birthplace

claims.text: UNESCO calls the Konark Sun Temple the culmination of Kalingan temple architecture, with all its defining elements in complete form.

quotes.quote: The Sun Temple is the culmination of Kalingan temple architecture, with all its defining elements in complete and perfect form.

claims.text: The Khajuraho temples in Madhya Pradesh were built in sandstone during the Chandella dynasty, which reached its apogee between 950 and 1050.

quotes.quote: The temples at Khajuraho were built during the Chandella dynasty, which reached its apogee between 950 and 1050.
Built in sandstone, each temple is elevated from its environs by a highly ornate terraced platform
The land abutting the monuments is managed jointly by the Revenue official (i.e., District Collector, State government of Madhya Pradesh) and the Archaeological Survey of India

claims.text: All surfaces of the Khajuraho temples are profusely carved with motifs depicting sacred and secular themes.

quotes.quote: All surfaces are profusely carved with anthropomorphic and non-anthropomorphic motifs depicting sacred and secular themes.

claims.text: The three Hoysala temples at Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura are built with chloritic schist and carry sculptural panels, carvings and artists' signatures.

quotes.quote: The three component parts are built with chloritic schist and reflect the features such as stellate plans, horizontal friezes of the adhisthana, artists' signatures, sculptural panels and carvings that became the hallmark of this period.
such as the loss of religious activities at the Hoysalesvara Temple in Halebidu and Keshava Temple in Somanathapura
A continuity of worship, rituals and festivals is to be noticed at Channakeshava Temple (Belur), since its inception in 1117 CE.

claims.text: The Hoysala style includes sculptural galleries of religious and epic stories and stone carvings that cover the entire exterior surface of the temples.

quotes.quote: a thematically arranged sculptural gallery of religious, epic, and other stories along the circumambulatory platform, extensive sculptures and stone carvings that cover the entire exterior surface

claims.text: UNESCO's summary says the Taj Mahal, a white marble mausoleum, was built in Agra between 1631 and 1648 by order of Shah Jahan.

quotes.quote: An immense mausoleum of white marble, built in Agra between 1631 and 1648 by order of the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan in memory of his favourite wife

claims.text: UNESCO's statement of value says construction of the Taj Mahal started in 1632 AD and was completed in 1648 AD.

quotes.quote: It was built by Mughal Emperor Shah Jahan in memory of his wife Mumtaz Mahal with construction starting in 1632 AD and completed in 1648 AD

claims.text: Masons, stone-cutters, inlayers and carvers for the Taj Mahal were requisitioned from the whole empire and from Central Asia and Iran.

quotes.quote: For its construction, masons, stone-cutters, inlayers, carvers, painters, calligraphers, dome builders and other artisans were requisitioned from the whole of the empire and also from the Central Asia and Iran.

claims.text: The Taj Mahal is built of brick-in-lime mortar veneered with red sandstone and marble, with inlay of precious and semi-precious stones.

quotes.quote: The building material used is brick-in-lime mortar veneered with red sandstone and marble and inlay work of precious/semi precious stones.

claims.text: UNESCO says the relief work in marble and the inlay of precious and semi-precious stones make the Taj Mahal a monument apart.

quotes.quote: The relief work in marble and inlay with precious and semi precious stones make it a monument apart.

claims.text: The octagonal marble lattice screen around the Taj Mahal cenotaphs is highly polished, and its frames are inlaid with precious stones representing flowers.

quotes.quote: The exquisite octagonal marble lattice screen encircling both cenotaphs is a piece of superb workmanship. It is highly polished and richly decorated with inlay work.
The borders of the frames are inlaid with precious stones representing flowers executed with wonderful perfection.

claims.text: White Makrana marble from Rajasthan, for which the Taj Mahal is known, is the first Global Heritage Stone Resource from India and from Asia.

quotes.quote: Taj Mahal, the iconic mausoleum, known for finest quality white Makrana Marble from Rajasthan

marble from Makrana in Rajasthan is now Asia's first Global Heritage Stone Resource (GHSR), as confirmed on July 19 by the International Union of Geological Sciences (IUGS)

claims.text: The Taj Mahal's main mausoleum is made entirely of Makrana marble, within a complex of many buildings in marble and red sandstone.

quotes.quote: The Taj mausoleum is part of the Taj Mahal complex which has numerous edifices built in marble and red sandstone.
The Main Mausoleum (all made in Makrana Marble)

claims.text: Makrana marble has been used in Humayun's Tomb in New Delhi, Akbar's Tomb at Sikandra, the Moti Masjid in Lahore and the Victoria Memorial.

quotes.quote: Iconic sites where it has been used include Humayun's Tomb in New Delhi, Akbar's Tomb in Sikandra, Agra; Dukhnivaran Sahib Gurdwara, Ludhiana; Sheikh Zayed Mosque in Abu Dhabi and Moti Masjid in Lahore.
Renowned worldwide for its fine quality that can be credited for the Taj Mahal's incredible beauty and the Victoria Memorial's grandeur

quotes.quote: With the wide-scale mining of these stones because of their usage in heritage buildings, preserves are threatened, says Kaur, calling for the practice to be stopped.
the secretary general of heritage stone subcommission Dolores Pereira says the GHSR status means that some quarries of these heritage stones need to be conserved.

quotes.quote: Semi-precious stones such as lapis-lazuli, agate, bloodstone, carnelian, jade and quartz are used alongside clay-slate, variegated yellow limestone and marble in the designs.

quotes.quote: a fascinating example of an Italian or Italian-inspired pietra dura panel appearing in a Mughal context is that of a tablet, dating to 1648, depicting the Greek mythological figure, Orpheus
set into the back wall of Shah Jahan's throne at the Diwan-i-Aam in the Red Fort in Delhi, along with 318 other panels of inlay.

quotes.quote: Said to have been originally developed and perfected by Florentine artists in sixteenth-century Italy, pietra dura, meaning "hard stone" in Italian

quotes.quote: The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan was a strong proponent of the technique, which had been adapted into the local Mughal style and came to be known as parchin kari, literally meaning 'driven in'.

Decorative plate with inlay of onyx, malachite, lapis and turquoise.

Dealing with sculpture, painting, carpentry, jewellery and design, Shilpa Shastras are a collective body of texts that are primarily occupied with the practice of art.

claims.text: Shilpa Shastra texts are dated individually, not collectively, and generally date to the early centuries of the second millennium CE.

quotes.quote: While most Shilpa texts were written in Sanskrit, some are written in regional and, rarely, even modern languages such as Hindi.

claims.text: The Vishnudharmottara Purana measures images in angulas, talas of twelve angulas and mukhas, and gives each figure a height of nine mukhas.

quotes.quote: The system proposed by the Vishnudharmottara Purana suggests three units of measurement based on the human body - angulas, referring to the distance between the first and second joints of a bent forefinger; talas, referring to twelve angulas; and mukhas
mukhas, spanning from the face's hairline to the chin
The height of each figure measured nine mukhas.

claims.text: The Shilpa texts set three requirements for every sculpted image: beauty, auspiciousness and verisimilitude.

quotes.quote: Broadly, the texts put forth three requirements that every sculpted image is meant to meet - beauty, auspiciousness and verisimilitude.

claims.text: The Shilpa texts treat broken or imperfect images as unfavourable, often attracting malevolent spirits.

quotes.quote: Broken or imperfect images are treated as unfavourable, often attracting malevolent spirits.

claims.text: The Shilpa Shastras ask a sculptor to pay respect to the stone and his tools and to meditate on the deity before beginning work.

quotes.quote: Shilpa Shastras state that a sculptor should pay respect to both the stone and his tools before commencing his work. Equally, he should meditate on the divine nature of the god or goddess he wishes to portray
Each stage of production is meant to be accompanied by rituals that aid the act of creation

claims.text: Scholars question how far Shilpa Shastra rules were followed, and Parker found master architects and sculptors who had never read them.

quotes.quote: scholars have questioned the extent to which their prescriptions were incorporated in works of art.
these texts illustrate the aspirational ideals but not the daily practise of image-making in which discrepansies are the norm.

He has also discovered that architects and sculptors who were considered masters in their work had never even read any written version of Shilpa Shastras in Sanskrit or in their local South Indian language

claims.text: By the Shilpa Shastras, deity carvings for temples keep their eyes unfinished until the eye-opening ceremony, when a master carves them with a golden needle chisel.

quotes.quote: According to Shilpa Shastras, those carvings of deities aimed for temple worship are left with their eyes unfinished or "closed", and they are only carved in the actual eye-opening ceremony
This is a task that only a master craftsman is allowed to perform and is made with a chisel known as a "golden needle'.

claims.text: Sivonen describes four classes of stone carvers, which primarily reflect temple construction: the master carver sthapati, the surveyor sutragrahim, the carver takshaka, and the builders, plasterers and painters called vardhakin.

quotes.quote: There are four classes of stone carvers. The master carver and design architect is called sthapati. Second to him is the surveyor sutragrahim, followed by the sculptor or the carver, known as takshaka in the third class.
Builders, plasterers and painters constitute the fourth class vardhakin.
These occupational categories primarily reflect temple construction procedures that also include making deity sculptures.

claims.text: Stone carvers in India are also known by the Sanskrit name shilpi, meaning an artist and a craftsman.

quotes.quote: The stone carvers in India are also known by the Sanskrit name shilpi that refers to an artist and a craftsman.

claims.text: Viswakarma is a pan-Indian caste group of sub-castes with hereditary art and craft occupations, also known by names such as achari and kammalar.

quotes.quote: Viswakarma is a general name for a pan-Indian caste group that includes several sub-castes or communities with different names and social statuses
There are also other common names that imply Viswakarma status such as achari and kammalar.
Many artist and craftsmen in India even today belong to the Viswakarma caste.
the Viswakarma caste group that is characterised by hereditary art and craft occupations

claims.text: A legend says the god Viswakarma had five sons, a blacksmith, a carpenter, a metal worker, a stone carver and a goldsmith.

quotes.quote: Legend states that the god Viswakarma, the god of arts and crafts, had five sons: a blacksmith, a carpenter, a metal worker, a stone carver and a goldsmith.

claims.text: Sivonen describes granite in Tamil Nadu being classed masculine, feminine or neutral by its sound when struck, and a Hoysala sculptor in Karnataka is taught to identify stones by their sound.

quotes.quote: Granite is particularly highly valued and used in the state of Tamil Nadu.
Depending on the sound of the stones when hit with a piece of metal, they can be defined as masculine, feminine or neutral.
In Karnataka, a Hoysala stone sculptor draws his creative technique from the wisdom of centuries. He is taught to identify stones on the basis of the sound they emit when beaten

claims.text: Masculine granite, called ansila, makes a clear, bell-like sound and is considered the best stone, with the fewest cracks, for statues of male deities.

quotes.quote: Masculine granite, called ansila, makes a clear, bell-like sound and it is considered to be the best quality of stone with the fewest cracks. Ansila is suitable for making statues of male deities.

claims.text: Female pensila granite sounds quieter, while neutral nabunsagar cracks most, sounds like a drum and is unsuitable for statues of worship.

quotes.quote: Pensila is the female granite stone for female deities, next in quality, and the sound is quieter. The worst in quality is the neutral stone nabunsagar that is most prone to cracking and makes a drum-like sound.
Neutral stones can be used for less important architectural parts but they are not suitable for making statues for religious worship.

claims.text: In Karnataka, male stones are used for sculpting gods, female stones for goddesses and neutral stones for objects.

quotes.quote: 'male stones' are used for sculpting gods, 'female stones' for goddesses, and 'neutral stones' for objects.

claims.text: The Government College of Architecture and Sculpture in Mamallapuram, Chengalpattu District, began in 1957 as a Sculpture Training Centre to revive sculpture and architecture.

quotes.quote: The Government College of Architecture and Sculpture is located in Mamallapuram, Chengalpattu District, Tamil Nadu.

It was started in 1957 as the Sculpture Training Centre under the guidance of Department of Industries and Commerce with a sole objective of reviving and extending the frontiers of age-old tradition of Sculpture and Architecture.
The Government College of Traditional Architecture and Sculpture was founded in 1957 and was affiliated to Madras University in Chennai.

claims.text: The Mamallapuram college teaches stone sculpture by the Shilpa Shastras, with a curriculum of Shilpa, Agama and Vastu Sastras and iconometry.

quotes.quote: its curriculum comprises Shilpa, Agama, Vastu Sastras, Iconometrical and Iconographical sketches of Sculptures, Aesthetics, Philosophy along with Sanskrit, English and Tamil.

the teaching of stone carving follows the guidance based on Shipa Shastras and students learn to design and make sculptures based on traditional guidelines of correct forms, measurements and iconography.

claims.text: Students at the Mamallapuram college start by carving ornaments in soft stones and work with granite in their final fourth year.

quotes.quote: During first-year studies, students learn drawing for stone, and work with soft stones making ornamentations such as flowers and animals.
During the final fourth year, students work with granite

claims.text: Sivonen found that, unlike the consistent tradition from the Pallava era that travel guides suggest, Mamallapuram's carving industry developed to its present state through the 1957 sculpture college and the town's growth as a tourist destination.

quotes.quote: Although many international travel guides give the impression that there has been a consistent, elaborate stone carving tradition in Mamallapuram from the Pallava era to the present day

in reality the stone carving industry has developed to its present state as a result of the establishment of the Government College of Sculpture and Traditional Architecture in Mamallapuram in 1957, and much in connection with the growth of Mamallapuram as a popular tourist destination

claims.text: With no official record, some estimates put Mamallapuram's workshops at over 200, and in September 2010 Sivonen counted 162 stone carving units in the town's main areas.

quotes.quote: There were no official record of the exact number of stone carving units or stone carvers working in Mamallapuram, but according to some estimates there were over 200 workshops in the town and thousands of stone carvers.
In September 2010 I counted 162 stone carving units in the main areas of the town.

claims.text: Mamallapuram's deity sculptures are made for Hindu temples and shrines around the world and also sold as souvenirs to international tourists.

quotes.quote: Deity sculptures are made for Hindu temples and shrines around the world but also to be sold as souvenirs for international tourists visiting Mamallapuram.

claims.text: Indian buyers were the main buyers of granite carvings, while soft stone statues were also bought by foreign tourists.

quotes.quote: Whereas Indian people were the main buyers of granite carvings for temples, shrines and for decoration, soft stone statues were also bought by foreign tourists.

claims.text: In 2010, salaried workers in Mamallapuram granite carving units earned on average 300 rupees a day, working eight hours a day, six days a week.

quotes.quote: On average people working in the granite carving units on a fixed salary earned 300 rupees per day in 2010. They worked on average eight hours a day, six days per week

claims.text: Mamallapuram stone carvers are exposed to stone dust, noise and accidents, used very little protective equipment, and many suffered eye and respiratory problems.

quotes.quote: There are many health hazards that the stone carvers become exposed to, such as stone dust, noise, and accidents from handling the stones and electric tools.
People used very little protective equipment in the workshops. The dust was the biggest problem and many carvers suffered from eye and respiratory problems.

claims.text: Most Mamallapuram carvers were registered as artisans with the Board of Handicrafts in Chennai and received an identity card and a health insurance card.

quotes.quote: Most carvers from Mamallapuram were registered as stone carvers, labelled as "artisans", in the Board of Handicrafts in Chennai. They received an identity card as well as a health insurance card

claims.text: Granite, an igneous rock, is still used for temple architecture and remains the main material for religious Hindu carvings in Tamil Nadu.

quotes.quote: Granite belongs to the group of igneous rocks.
Granite is still used for temple architecture and it continues to be the main material for religious Hindu carvings in Tamil Nadu.

claims.text: Granite deposits are abundant in South India, so many temples and sculptures there have been made of granite throughout the centuries.

quotes.quote: In South India, including Tamil Nadu, granite deposits are found in abundance in the ground and as a result of this many of the temples and sculptures have been made in granite throughout the centuries.

claims.text: The stone mostly used in Mamallapuram granite sculpture, called black granite, was a slightly softer version of granite called blue metal, 25 per cent basalt, which holds details better than dense granite.

quotes.quote: the stone mostly used in Mamallapuram granite sculpture and usually referred to as black granite was actually a slightly softer version of granite that was called blue metal. Blue metal is 25 per cent basalt stone
The carvers valued its qualities since it holds the details better than the high density granite and can also be carved by hand if necessary.

claims.text: In 2010, granite for Mamallapuram carving cost around 40,000 rupees per cubic metre, while blue metal cost 10,000 rupees.

quotes.quote: In Mamallapuram, pure granite and blue metal were both used for temple construction, religious sculptures as well as for making monumental statues only for decoration.
Whereas real granite would cost around 40,000 rupees per cubic metre (about 580 euro in 2010), blue metal costs 10,000 rupees (about 150 euro).

claims.text: Soft stones are often called soapstones because some of them contain talc, which feels soapy in the hands.

quotes.quote: Soft stones are often called soap stones as some of them contain talc that can produce a soapy feeling in hands when touched.

claims.text: Soft stones vary in hardness: some take a very high level of detail, while some very soft stones break very easily when carved.

quotes.quote: There are different varieties of soft stones that vary in their degree of hardness. Some soft stones can take on a very high level of detail
Some very soft stones produce a risk when carved as they can break very easily.

claims.text: Gadapa stone, also called durgi stone, a plain grey soft stone quarried in Andhra Pradesh, was the cheapest and softest stone carved in Mamallapuram.

quotes.quote: Gadapa stone used to be the most popular soft stone in Mamallapuram tourist carving units and it was quarried in the state of Andra Pradesh. Another name for it is durgi stone
However, it was the cheapest and softest stone variety, is easy to carve and was typically used for the Mamallapuram tourist market.
The colour of gadapa stone is very plain grey without shade variations, even when polished

claims.text: In 2010, gadapa stone used in Mamallapuram cost around 150-250 rupees per square foot, and green stone from Bangalore around 250-300 rupees.

quotes.quote: The soft stone mainly used in Mamallapuram carving units that produce carvings for the tourist market were gadapa stone and a so-called green stone.
In 2010 the price for gadapa stone was around 150-250 rupees per square foot (around 3-4 euro).
Green stone came from Bangalore (now Bengaluru) in the state of Karnataka, and it cost around 250-300 rupees per square foot in 2010

claims.text: During Sivonen's fieldwork, red and yellow marble from Rajasthan and near Agra was the most popular stone for Mamallapuram souvenirs, replacing gadapa stone.

quotes.quote: In Mamallapuram red and yellow marble were the most commonly used types.
Marble came from North India, from the state of Rajasthan and near the city of Agra in the state of Uttar Pradesh.
During my fieldwork marble was the most popular stone for the souvenir sculptures to use and had replaced gadapa stone in recent years.

claims.text: A Mamallapuram stone carver's main hand tools were a hand saw, a pen, hammers, chisels of many types, polishing stones and emery paper.

quotes.quote: The main hand tools of a stone carver were a hand saw, a pen, hammers, a variety of different type of chisels, polishing stones and emery paper.

claims.text: Electric saws, drills and grinders entered Mamallapuram carving in the 1990s for granite and big pieces, but detailing was still done by hand.

quotes.quote: Mechanical aids such as electric saws, drills and grinders were introduced to the business in the 1990s and were used for granite and big soft stone sculptures.
granite carvings were made mainly with electric tools since it saves time and labour, but detailing was still done by hand.

claims.text: In Mamallapuram, soft stone carvings were made primarily by hand, since many soft stones are unsuitable for machinery and break easily.

quotes.quote: Soft stone carvings were produced primarily by hand unless electric aids were needed for cutting the stone or the stone happened to be very hard. However, many soft stones are unsuitable for machinery since they break easily.
Stone carvings in Mamallapuram were produced by using both hand and electric tools.

claims.text: In Mamallapuram, carving started with rough cutting the stone to size, then drawing the statue on the block and cutting off the extra stone around the image.

quotes.quote: The procedure referred as rough cutting consisted of cutting a stone into the size that is desired for the carving.
After this the carver drew an image of the statue on the surface of the block of stone.
any further extra pieces of stone around the image were cut off with the help of a electric or hand saw and hammer.
The process of stone carving started with the basic dressing of the stone.
Stone carvings in Mamallapuram were produced by using both hand and electric tools.

claims.text: Mamallapuram carvers kept the stone flat on the ground for most of the carving, which prevented accidents and breakage.

quotes.quote: Throughout the whole process of basic dressing, the stone laid flat on the ground. Most of the carving was also done by keeping the stone in this position as it prevented accidents and possible breakage of the stone.

claims.text: A Mamallapuram carver controlled the outcome of the carving by manipulating the angle of the chisel and the force of the hammer blow.

quotes.quote: By manipulating the angle of the chisel and the force used in hammering, he could control the outcome of the carving.
Stone carvings in Mamallapuram were produced by using both hand and electric tools.

claims.text: In Mamallapuram, the whole statue was usually worked layer by layer, from the sketch to the rough shape and then to the final finishing touches.

quotes.quote: Usually the whole statue was worked on layer by layer so that the carving proceeded as a whole from the sketching of the image to the rough shape and then to the final finishing touches.
Stone carvings in Mamallapuram were produced by using both hand and electric tools.

claims.text: Gujarat's beads have mostly been made from stone of the agate beds along the Narmada River, with the former Rajpipla State prominent in producing it.

quotes.quote: the beads manufactured in Gujarat have been made, for the most part, from stone found in the agate beds along the banks of the Narmada River
The erstwhile Princely State of Rajpipla has been particularly prominent in the production of this raw material.

claims.text: The agates come from the Deccan Trap lava flows, eroded over millennia from the basalt into the rivers and concentrated into workable beds.

quotes.quote: The agates are associated with the Deccan Trap of central and western India, a series of Mesozoic lava flows which cover an immense area of the subcontinent.
Over the millennia the high silica content stones have been eroded from the interstices of the basalt trap rock, from where they have entered the riverine system.
There are extensive strata of these agates which have been concentrated by fluvial processes into workable beds of stone.

claims.text: Agate nodules are extracted with picks and shovels; in the community Possehl visited, the work force was teams of three to five men and women, and women sorted the agates.

quotes.quote: The extraction of the nodules is done with picks and shovels. In the community I visited the work force was made up of teams of three to five men and women.
After the pans were dumped near the opening of the access hole, women sorted the valuable agates from the undesirable material

claims.text: The agate miners Possehl met at the Narmada were of African descent, people called Siddis in western India and Pakistan.

quotes.quote: The people who mine the stones, in this locality at least, are of African descent.
Such people are actually more common than one might suspect in western India and Pakistan, especially the coastal areas, where they are called Siddis.

claims.text: Possehl reported that the Narmada River agate mines were owned by the Government of India and that the Siddis had to purchase a lease to dig for stones.

quotes.quote: The Narmada River agate mines are owned by the Government of India and the Siddis have to purchase a lease to dig for the stones.

claims.text: In Cambay the raw agate is first heated in small pots of smouldering sawdust, a physical change in the stone that makes chipping easier.

quotes.quote: The first step in the process is to heat the material in small pots filled with smoldering sawdust (Fig. 4). This causes a physical change in the stone which makes the next step, chipping, an easier one.

claims.text: Cambay beads are chipped with a water buffalo horn hammer on a bamboo handle against a spike in the ground, and cow horn is unsuitable.

quotes.quote: the technique involves the use of a hammer and spike, or anvil, driven into the ground. The rough chipping hammer is made of water buffalo horn on a thin flexible bamboo handle.
It was made clear to me that the horn must be buffalo and that the horn of cows was completely unsuitable.

claims.text: In Cambay all chipping was done by men, while the bead grinding workshops employed both men and women.

quotes.quote: all of the chipping is done by males
The work force here, however, is composed of both males and females

claims.text: Cambay bead blanks are ground on commercially made abrasive wheels powered by electric motors, one of few machines in the industry.

quotes.quote: The abrasive wheels against which the beads are ground are commercially made today and powered by electric motors. This is one of the few applications of a mechanical contrivance in the Cambay bead industry.

claims.text: Cambay beads are perforated with a diamond-tipped bit set in a wooden shank and driven by a bow.

quotes.quote: Perforation is accomplished with a diamond-tipped bit set in a wooden shank and propelled by a bow.

claims.text: Water dripping from a small clay pot lubricates the drill, and the grit gathering in it seemingly furthers cutting through abrasion.

quotes.quote: The small clay pots seen in the photographs hold water and the grit from past drillings. This acts as a lubricant for the cutting operation.

The grit, which steadily accumulates in this water, is seemingly also an important commodity since its presence in the cutting hole would produce some abrasion and hence further the penetration of the stone.

claims.text: Every bead is drilled from one end and completed from the other, which Possehl reads as safer than drilling straight through.

quotes.quote: No matter how small the bead, the drilling is always started from one end and completed by drilling a second hole from the opposite side.
I interpret this procedure as a safer course of action than drilling straight through the bead, which might cause breakage and shatter around the exit hole.

claims.text: Beads are polished by turning them for approximately a week in drums with a coarse and then a finer abrasive slurry.

quotes.quote: The beads are placed in a drum with an abrasive slurry (Fig. 12), and continuously turned until their surfaces have been smoothed and polished. This takes approximately a week.
The Cambay process involves a first turning in slurry with a coarse abrasive, and a second session with a finer powder.

claims.text: Cambay's lapidaries use stone from across India and neighbouring countries, including Afghan lapis lazuli, Tamil Nadu rose quartz and Karnataka fuchsite.

quotes.quote: The modern Cambay lapidary industry makes use of stone from most, if not all, of the regions of India and adjacent countries.
Lapis lazuli from the Badakshan region of Afghanistan is as much used as is rose quartz from Tamil Nadu. There are also fuchsite from Karnataka

claims.text: Agate workers, locally called Akik workers, in the Khambhat region of Anand district are at potential risk of exposure to a high amount of silica dust from grinding agate.

quotes.quote: Agate workers (locally known as "Akik" workers) in the Khambhat region of the Anand district of Gujarat state in India are at potential risk of exposure to high amount of silica dust due to grinding of agate stones in their occupation.

claims.text: Agate is ground on emery grinding wheels turning at 2,000-3,000 rpm, which generates a large amount of dust.

quotes.quote: Agate stone grinding is done on grinding wheels (emery) at a speed of 2,000-3,000 rpm, which generates a large amount of dust.

claims.text: The dust from agate grinding contains fine particles 2-5 micron in size that reach the alveoli when inhaled.

quotes.quote: The dust contains fine dust particles of 2-5 micron in size which when inhaled reach the alveoli

claims.text: One study found respirable dust in household agate units about 15-fold higher than the permissible level.

quotes.quote: A study revealed that the respirable dust concentration in household units is about 15-fold higher (2.35-2.74 mg/m3) than the permissible level (0.16 mg/m3)

claims.text: Inhaled silica dust induces silicosis, and long-term exposure raises susceptibility to tuberculosis and the risk of lung cancer.

quotes.quote: Inhalation of silica dust (SiO2) is known to induce silicosis among exposed workers.
Long-term exposure leads to development of silicosis and increased susceptibility to tuberculosis5) and to a higher risk of developing lung cancer6).

claims.text: Interviews with 82 Khambhat agate workers in 2010 to 2011 found 80% knew of dust-preventive methods but only 22% used them.

quotes.quote: The interviews were conducted among 82 agate workers out of about 215 agate workers in three villages, Metpur, Sakarpur, and Timba in the Khambhat region of Gujarat state in India
The interviews were conducted from June 2010 to July 2011.
knew about simple preventive methods to avoid silica dust exposure (80%), but only a minority of the workers (22%) were actually using the simple and available dust-preventive methods.

claims.text: The simple dust-preventive methods known to agate workers were wet grinding and a mask made by covering the face with layers of cloth.

quotes.quote: knew about the simple and easily available preventive methods of wet grinding or use of a mask (covering of face with layers of cloths) to reduce silica dust exposure

claims.text: The reasons agate workers most commonly gave for not using a preventive method were that it felt uncomfortable and inconvenient.

quotes.quote: The most common cited reasons for not using a preventive method were feeling uncomfortable and inconvenient to use.

claims.text: In the Khambhat survey, 28% of workers with 5 or more years of schooling used preventive methods, against only 9% of uneducated workers.

quotes.quote: 28% of the workers with 5 years or more of schooling were using the preventive methods, 24% of the workers with less than five years of schooling were using preventive methods, and only 9% of the uneducated (no schooling) workers were using preventive methods

claims.text: Women were 57% of the agate workers surveyed in 2010 to 2011, and the author suggests more women might prefer agate work as a household industry.

quotes.quote: There were slightly more female workers (57%) than male workers (43%). Being a household industry, more women might prefer to work in the agate industry.
The interviews were conducted from June 2010 to July 2011.

claims.text: Most agate units have no exhaust systems, and most workers use no dust-preventive methods and remain at risk of silica exposure.

quotes.quote: Still, most of the agate units have no exhaust systems, and most of the workers do not use any dust-preventive methods and remain at risk of significant silica-dust

claims.text: Agate workers are usually involved in stone cutting, stone grinding and polishing work on agate stones for ornaments and jewellery.

quotes.quote: Agate workers are usually involved in various processes, including stone cutting, stone grinding, and polishing work on agate stones for ornamental and jewellery

claims.text: Citing an earlier study, Chaudhury and colleagues report that about 38% of workers in India's agate stone polishing industries develop silicosis in their lifetime.

quotes.quote: In Agate stone polishing industries of India, about 38% of workers develop silicosis in their lifetime.[2]

claims.text: Chaudhury and colleagues cite a study finding that families and other non-occupational residents of agate polishing areas also develop silicosis, at 6.8 - 11.8 %.

quotes.quote: their families and other nonoccupational groups that also reside within the area develop silicosis (6.8 - 11.8 %), Silico-tuberculosis (2.8 - 6.3%), and tuberculosis (TB) (19.7 - 20.1%).[3]

claims.text: Studies cited by Chaudhury and colleagues found respirable dust in the household agate industries very high in concentration, with more than 60% free silica.

quotes.quote: Studies reveal that the concentration of respirable dust in these household industries is very high and contains more than 60% free silica in it.

claims.text: Of 53 chest-symptomatic agate workers at Shakarpur, enrolled in 2007 and followed for 30 months, thirteen died in less than 3 years of follow-up.

quotes.quote: Spirometry for lung function, chest X-ray, anthropometry, body fat % measurement, record of tuberculosis status and ILO classification of pneumoconiosis were done among 53 chest symptomatic patients above 15 years of age who were followed for 30 months.
who attended a specially arranged health clinic for the agate workers at Shakarpur on invitation, from June to December 2007 and were followed up till March 2010
Thirteen participants died in less than 3 years of follow up.

claims.text: The Shakarpur agate workers who died were aged 28 to 60 years, with both mean and median at 40 years.

quotes.quote: The age at death of the participants ranges from 28 years to 60 years, with both mean and median at 40 years.

claims.text: Tuberculosis and nutritional status strongly influenced mortality among the Shakarpur agate workers, and over half the men were underweight at enrolment.

quotes.quote: On regression analysis, TB and nutritional status were found to have strong influence on mortality.
more than half of the male workers were underweight (BMI<18.5 kg/m2) at enrollment

claims.text: Chaudhury and colleagues wrote that in Shakarpur, in Khambhat subdivision, unorganized labourers had been making ornaments and decorative items from agate and other stones for several decades.

quotes.quote: In Shakarpur of Khambhat subdivision of Gujarat, India, unorganized laborers have been making ornaments and other decorative and showcase items from agate and other stones since several decades.

claims.text: Jha gives the composition of soapstone as talk (talc), mica, chlorite, carbonate, amphibole and other natural minerals.

quotes.quote: Chemical composition of soapstone includes talk, mica, chlorite, carbonate, amphibole and other natural minerals.

claims.text: Soapstone is nonporous, nonabsorbent, a low conductor of electricity, heat resistant, of high specific heat capacity, and resistant to acids and alkalis.

quotes.quote: Among physical qualities, soapstone is a- nonporous, nonabsorbent, low conductor of electricity, heat resistant, higher specific heat capacity, resistant to acid and alkaline substances.

claims.text: Jha writes that a high amount of talk (talc) in its composition makes soapstone soft and craft-friendly.

quotes.quote: Due to higher amount of talk, as its basic composition, soapstone displays, soft and craft-friendly

claims.text: Several soapstone mines around Dhakotha in Kendujhar district keep the Dhakotha craft cluster self-dependent for raw material.

quotes.quote: As, there are several soapstone mines available around Dhakotha area, which is situated in Kendujhar districtxv, so, this feature makes Dhakotha craft cluster, selfdependent regarding continuous raw material availability.

claims.text: Dhakotha craftsmen use blackish grey, pink, orange, light green and dark green soapstone.

quotes.quote: blackish grey, pink, orange, light green and dark green colored soapstone are used for craftsmanship purposes.

claims.text: Soft granite, dark grey and harder than soapstone, is not suitable for carving at Dhakotha but is ideal for Patthar Kundo turning.

quotes.quote: 06. Soft Granite Visually dark grey with blackish tone in color composition. Grain marks are difficult to identify. Harder than soapstone. Not suitable for carving, but Ideal for Patthar Kundo.
Table-1: Raw soapstone used by craftsmen in Dhakotha

claims.text: Patthar Kundo turning uses a handmade wooden lathe worked by two craftsmen, one pulling a rope to roll the axis while the other carves the stone with carving tools.

quotes.quote: The wooden, handmade wooden lathe system is developed by the craft community members themselves and being used for craftsmanship purposes.

The first craftsman holds the pulling rope in his both hands and perform axis rolling in clockwise and in anticlockwise direction; while the another craftsman preforms stone carving process, with the help of different carving tools.

claims.text: In Patthar Kundo the stone is glued to the turning bar with glue from Kusum trees, Schleichera oleosa, heated to bond and heated again to release.

quotes.quote: This glue is collected from locally available Kulsum or Kusum
Botanical name of this tree is- Schleichera Oleosa, and belongs to the family of Sapindaceae.
Stage-H: Pre-turning heating, to achieve stronger glue bounding, between soapstone and turning-bar's head end.
Stage-L: Post-turning heating process, to un-glue the turned form.

claims.text: At the 2010-2011 study, soapstone carving had existed in Dhakotha for around 55-60 years, newer than the Patthar Kundo turning craft.

quotes.quote: Soapstone carving is respectively a newer soapstone craft in Dhakotha area with around 55-60 year's existence in this area.
This craft study cum design intervention initiative was conducted during 2010-2011 by this author.

claims.text: Dhakotha carvers use chisels, hammers, mallets, a jute chatti cushion and a wooden lakdi pidha support that keeps sharp edges from chipping.

quotes.quote: Among tools- chisel, hammer, mallet, Lakdi Pidha, Jute Chatti etc. are commonly used by craftsmen for carving soapstone statues and other carved products.
Provides angular support and cushioning to the under process stone products and prevent their sharp edges from unexpected chippings

claims.text: Because pencil marks might erase during chiselling, Dhakotha carvers turn the drawn lines into surface-etched lines with a fine-tipped chisel.

quotes.quote: As the HB pencil marks might erase during the soapstone chiseling process, so, craftsmen convert, final pencil drawn line marks, into the surface-etched line marks, with the help of a fine tipped chisel.

claims.text: Sandpaper gives carved stone its final finish in Dhakotha soapstone carving and in Karnataka icon carving, where it is followed by coconut oil.

quotes.quote: Application of sand paper over a chiseled surface, to achieve final finishing.
The final image is then smoothened with sandpaper and rubbed with coconut oil.

claims.text: Dhakotha carvers make statues of Hindu gods and goddesses and architectural, decorative and household utility products, while Patthar Kundo makes utensils.

quotes.quote: Mostly, statues of different Hindu gods, goddesses for religious purposes; architectural decorative and household daily-utility based soapstone products are being crafted by the carving craft community members.
In Patthar Kundo craft, different forms of utensils are being crafted, while in soapstone carving craft, highly detailed soapstone statue crafting takes place.

claims.text: The sculptures of the Konark temple's Jaga Mohan and Natya Mandir are carved in khondalite, called Kanda pathar in Oriya.

quotes.quote: a. Khondalite, "Kanda pathar" in Oriya for the main temple Jaga Mohan, and Natya Mandir, endowed with engraved sculptors.
with its sculptural embellishment carved in khondalitic rock.

claims.text: The term khondalite, from the Kond tribe of Odisha, was coined by T. L. Walker in 1902 for rocks of quartz, felspar, garnet and sillimanite.

quotes.quote: The khondalite term, derived from the Kond (also called Khond) tribe of Odisha, was first coined by T. L. Walker (1902) for the rocks having mineralogy such as quartz, felspar, garnet, and sillimanite.

claims.text: Khondalite was chosen at Konark for its availability nearby and because it was easier to sculpt than laterite.

quotes.quote: The choice of khondalite is due to its availability in the vicinity and preference over laterite for ease of sculpting.

claims.text: The exact source of the khondalite used at Konark and how it was carried to the site are yet to be deciphered.

quotes.quote: However, the exact source of the rocks used and their mode of transport from the source to the construction site is yet to be deciphered.

claims.text: Mohapatra names Narsingpur and Tapanga as possible sources of Konark's khondalite, carried by the waterways of the Mahanadi.

quotes.quote: Narsingpur and Tapanga are possible sources of khondalite. If it is Narsinghpur, the transport is only through the waterways of Mahanadi and its distributary system

claims.text: At the Konark temple, laterite was used for the foundations and side walls.

quotes.quote: Out of the three types of rocks, laterite is used for foundations and side walls.

claims.text: Mohapatra writes that green chlorite, locally muguni, was used at Konark for the simhasan, cult icons, occasionally door frames, and the main deity Surya.

quotes.quote: The ultrabasic rocks commonly known as chlorite (locally 'muguni') are used for simhasan, cult icons, and occasionally for door frames, and the main deity "Surya" (Behera, 2005).
These are invariably green in colour and fine-grained

claims.text: The Athgarh sandstone found around Bhubaneswar has been used to build all the temples of Bhubaneswar since the 7th century AD.

quotes.quote: The Upper Gondwana sandstones of Odisha (Athgarh Sandstone) that occur in and around Bhubaneswar have been extensively used in the construction of all the temples of Bhubaneswar since the 7th century AD

claims.text: Konark's khondalite weathers mainly as its feldspars and red almandine garnet alter to kaolinite and goethite, disfiguring the sculptures.

quotes.quote: Textural observations indicated that the main weathering reaction was the alteration of feldspars and red garnet (almandine) to kaolinite and goethite (Raymahashay and Sharma, 1993).
Mostly alteration of minerals of feldspars and garnets has given rise to the disfiguring of the sculptors.

claims.text: Salt air at Konark has eroded the metal cramps supporting the temple, and airborne saline water could be a reason the sculptures are disfigured.

quotes.quote: erosion of metal cramps supporting the structure due to salt air has in the past resulted in some damage.
its nearness to the sea could be a reason for the disfigurement of the artistic sculptors due to airborne saline water.

claims.text: The EPCH report ranks Odisha's carving stones from soft white Khadipathara soapstone through Kochilapathara chlorite and khondalite to the hardest, black Mugunipathara granite.

quotes.quote: are enough to carve the ultra soft white soapstone, or Khadipathara, harder greenish chlorite or Kochilapathara and pinkish Khandolite or Sahanapathara or Baulapathara and the hardest of all black granite or Mugunipathara.

claims.text: Odisha carvers need only simple hammers and chisels of various shapes and sizes, known locally as muna, patili, martual, thuk-thuki and nihana.

quotes.quote: Only a few simple tools like hammers and chisels of various shapes and sizes better known as 'Muna', 'Patili', 'Martual', ;Thuk-Thuki' and 'Nihana' in local parlance

claims.text: The EPCH report says Odisha's stone work differs from other places in being carved, instead of hard marble, on a soft pink stone from the Barbil areas, available only in small pieces.

quotes.quote: The stone work of odisha is very different from other places.Instead of hard marble,carving is done on a soft stone called pink stone - a stone brought from the barbil areas.
Due to its softness,only small pieces of pink stone are available,thereby,limiting the size of its end products.

claims.text: In Odisha, carvings are hand polished with a traditional powder applied with moist muslin, and final polishing uses zinc powder.

quotes.quote: Hand polishing of the base article is done using a traditional polishing powder which is applied on the surface with a soft, moist muslin cloth.
The final polishing is done using zinc powder.

claims.text: The EPCH report describes Odisha's stone carvers as descendants of the builders of the Lingaraj, Jagannath and Konark temples.

quotes.quote: It was evolved over centuries by craftsmen who are descendants of the great builders of the famous temples of Lingaraj, Jaganntha, Konark, Rajarani and other temples

claims.text: Craftsmen in Pathuriasahi at Puri carve replicas of temple sculptures in soft pink stone and hard kochila.

quotes.quote: Craftsmen in Pathuriasahi at Puri use soft pinkstone and hard kochila to carve replicas of temple sculptures.

claims.text: In Karnataka icon carving, a sketch drawn on the sized stone is roughed out with steel rods and mallets, then finished with chisels and files.

quotes.quote: After the raw stone is selected and sized, a sketch of the proposed image is drawn on to it. This is realised roughly with the help of steel rods and mallets.
The sculpture is brought to its final form with chisels of varied sizes and its roughness is polished away with files of increasing sharpness.

claims.text: The UP MSME portal describes Banda's shazar as using a wooden bow with a delicate steel wire called kaman, with stones mounted on a wooden khunta stand and cut with silicon carbide powder.

quotes.quote: Shazar, uniquely crafted in Banda, India, features a traditional design using a wooden bow and a delicate steel wire known as 'Kaman.' Stones are mounted on a wooden stand called 'khunta' and cut with silicon carbide powder.

claims.text: Banda's district administration says shajar stone, also called fungus or tree augite, is found only in the Ken River and shows leaf or tree patterns.

quotes.quote: ODOP known as Shajar, Fungus Augite, or Tree Augite. This stone is found exclusively in the Ken River and has fossils of fungus inside it that resemble patterns of leaves or trees

claims.text: Banda, a district in the Bundelkhand region of Uttar Pradesh, has shajar stone as its ODOP product, used mainly for making jewellery.

quotes.quote: Banda, a district in the Bundelkhand region of Uttar Pradesh having a rich historical tradition going back to the remote antiquity. It prominently known for ODOP Shajar stone, which is used for making jewellery
Shajar stone is primarily used for making exquisite jewelry and has gained popularity across the country.

claims.text: Uttar Pradesh's MSME department notes that modern stone workshops may use CNC machines or laser cutters to complement handwork.

quotes.quote: They are often handmade, though modern workshops may use tools like CNC machines or laser cutters to complement manual craftsmanship.

claims.text: The Varanasi statement of case calls its soft stone a kind of limestone, a metamorphic rock scientifically known as pyrophyllite.

quotes.quote: Soft Stone is the most appealing of the kinds of lime stones found in the country. It is a "Metamorphic Rock" and also known as 'PYROPHYLLITE", its scientific name.

claims.text: The same statement says marble is the hardest form of limestone and soapstone the softest and easiest to work.

quotes.quote: While Marble is the hardest form of limestone, Soap Stone is the softest and is easy to work on.

claims.text: The Varanasi statement says soft stone has no homogeneity of colour, tint and texture, so two pieces from the same block are never alike.

quotes.quote: there is no homogeneity of colour, tint and texture in soft stone. Two pieces taken out, even from the same block of soft stone, are never alike.

claims.text: The Varanasi statement names marble, gorara soapstone and occasionally cuddapah as the base materials of stone craft in Uttar Pradesh.

quotes.quote: The base material of stone craft in Uttar Pradesh is marble, gorara soapstone and occasionally cuddapah.

claims.text: The Varanasi statement says carvers sprinkle water on the stone because friction from constant chiselling heats up the tools.

quotes.quote: Water is sprinkled repeatedly to avoid heat generation.
The craftsmen, sprinkle water on the stone during the course oftheir work because ofthe friction generated due to the constant chiseling away ofthe unwanted material results in the tools heating up.

claims.text: The Varanasi statement says that before carving the stone is kept in boiling water overnight and treated chemically, which smoothens and whitens its surface.

quotes.quote: Before carving the stone is kept in boiling water overnight and treated chemically. This smoothens and whitens the surface ofthe stone.

claims.text: Varanasi soft stone carvings are polished with sand or carborundum and finished with sandpaper, multani mitti or clay, oil and cloth.

quotes.quote: Polishing is done for the final finishing with sand or carborundum pieces.
Finishing is accomplished in a variety of ways from sand-papering, polishing with multani-mitti or clay, oil and cloth.

claims.text: The Varanasi statement says unwanted stone is chiselled out of harder stones, while in softer stones it is scraped out with a sharp flat-edged iron tool.

quotes.quote: while for the harder stones this is done by chiseling out the extra material, with softer stones. This is done by scraping out the same with a sharp flat-edged iron tool.

claims.text: The Varanasi statement names Ramnagar in Varanasi district, Luxa, Mishir Pokhra and Lahartara among the areas of soft stone cutwork.

quotes.quote: The base material of stone craft in Uttar Pradesh is marble, gorara soapstone and occasionally cuddapah. Ramnagar (a part of Varanasi district), Luxa, Mishir Pokhra, Lahartara and Samath is important geographical area for the soft stone under cutwork

claims.text: The Varanasi statement says soft stones are excavated from open mines, and large boulders are carried to workshops to be shaped by craftsmen.

quotes.quote: Soft Stones are excavated from open mines, Large sized boulders are carried to the workshops where they are given desired shapes and sizes by skilled and seasoned craftsmen.

claims.text: In most places carvers use local stone varieties, owing to lower transport costs, which affect the price of the raw material.

quotes.quote: in most places the local varieties are mostly used due to lower transport costs, which affect the price of the raw material.

claims.text: Possehl wrote that Cambay craftsmen have probably tried almost anything in stone, including ashtrays, paper weights, plaques, dishes, bowls, spoons and figurines.

quotes.quote: In fact almost anything that one might think of has probably been tried at least once, including ashtrays, paper weights, plaques, cigarette holders, dishes, bowls, spoons and figurines.

claims.text: Sivonen writes that soft stones are easier to carve than granite and easy to carve by hand, while granite and blue metal need more force and different tools because they are much harder.

quotes.quote: Soft stones are easier to carve than granite and are easy to carve by hand. Granite and blue metal, on the other hand, require more force and different tools since the material is much harder.

claims.text: Marble is a metamorphic rock but a hard stone, and its many varieties vary in colour and hardness.

quotes.quote: Marble is also a metamorphic rock but a hard stone. There are many different varieties of marble that vary in colour and hardness.

claims.text: Sivonen writes that the Shilpa Shastras are contained principally in the Citralakshana and the Citrasutra, whose exact dating is not clear but which is currently believed to date to the 5th century CE.

quotes.quote: Shilpa Shastras are contained principally in two texts, the Citralakshana and the Citrasutra that is a section of Vishnudharmottara-purana.
Their exact dating is not clear but Citrasutra is a supplement to Vishnupurana that is currently believed to date to the 5th century CE.

claims.text: Sivonen writes that these factors, the classing of granite by its sound among them, are considered general characteristics of Hindu stone carving but mainly show the ideals behind the work.

quotes.quote: Depending on the sound of the stones when hit with a piece of metal, they can be defined as masculine, feminine or neutral.
Although these factors presented above are considered to be general characteristics of Indian Hindu arts and stone carving, they mainly show the ideals behind the work.

claims.text: UNESCO names a Hassan District Committee for the Channakeshava Temple at Belur and the Hoysalesvara Temple at Halebidu, and a Mysuru District Committee for the Keshava Temple at Somanathapura.

quotes.quote: the Hassan District Committee for Channakeshava Temple and Hoysalesvara Temple; and the Mysuru District Committee for Keshava Temple
such as the loss of religious activities at the Hoysalesvara Temple in Halebidu and Keshava Temple in Somanathapura
A continuity of worship, rituals and festivals is to be noticed at Channakeshava Temple (Belur), since its inception in 1117 CE.

claims.text: In the banded khondalite used at Konark, feldspar-rich bands are conspicuously altered by kaolinitisation and garnet crystals are dislodged by alteration at their margins.

quotes.quote: The banding of segregated minerals is common with color contrast in used khondalite.
Felspathic bandings are conspicuously altered by kaolinitisation
Garnet crystals are dislodged due to margin alteration.

claims.text: Mohapatra describes laterite as a porous, pitted, clay-like rock formed by in situ alteration in tropical climates, with a hard limonitic crust holding much iron oxide and some aluminium oxide.

quotes.quote: Laterite, a typical derivative of in situ alteration from variable original parent rocks under tropical climatic conditions, is a porous, pitted, and clay-like rock with a hard, limonitic protective crust containing a substantial quantity of iron oxide and some aluminum oxide.

claims.text: Mohapatra writes that Konark's structures of chloritised or serpentinised mafic rock are better preserved and not prone to weathering or grain decay.

quotes.quote: The structures made up of chloritized or serpentinised mafic are better preserved and not prone to weathering or grain decay.

claims.text: Mohapatra notes that Ganguly in 1912 held Konark's dark green rock to be not chlorite but serpentinous or hornblendic, possibly brought from the Nilagiri hills.

quotes.quote: Ganguly (1912) opined that the rock is not chlorite; the dark green rock is serpentinous or hornblendic, possibly brought from Nilagiri hills near the villages of Santragodia and Goojadeeha.

claims.text: Live History India writes that Humayun is credited with introducing inlay to Mughal architecture, citing the Qila-i-Kuhna Mosque of 1540 CE as one of the earliest inlay works in India.

quotes.quote: Humayun, the second Mughal emperor, is credited with introducing inlay as a significant feature of Mughal architecture. The Qila-i-Kuhna Mosque in Delhi's Purana Qila (1540 CE) showcases one of the earliest examples of inlay work in India

claims.text: Outlook Traveller describes inlay stones being cut and shaped with a hand-operated machine while the marble is chiselled with a diamond-tipped chisel.

quotes.quote: To make a marble inlay artefact, the stones are cut and shaped with a hand-operated machine while the marble is chiselled with a diamond-tipped chisel.

claims.text: Inlay stones are set piece by piece into the carved-out marble and held with an adhesive whose recipe, artisans claim, is a trade secret, and the surface is then polished.

quotes.quote: then set piece by piece into the carved out marble, and held in place using an adhesive
a trade secret, the artisans claim
After the inlay is complete, the marble is buffed out and polished.
Once the stones are set using a special adhesive, the surface is scrubbed and polished to perfection.

claims.text: Live History India calls inlay artisans parachinkars and says they carve intricate grooves into marble, into which semi-precious stones are carefully inlaid.

quotes.quote: Artisans, known as parachinkars, carve intricate grooves into marble, into which semi-precious stones are carefully inlaid.

claims.text: The Mahabalipuram Stone Sculpture GI application, as the GI journal advertises it, says the techniques of Mamallapuram's Pallava monuments are still practised by its present sculptors.

quotes.quote: The techniques used in these historic pieces of art are still practised by the present sculptors of Mamallapuram.

claims.text: The Mahabalipuram Stone Sculpture GI application says the sculpture is made of pure granite using methods inscribed by the Pallavas: the Athama rules, Shilpa Shastras and Vastu Shastras.

quotes.quote: The sculpture is made out of pure granite using the methods inscribed by the Pallavas which seems to be evidently used in their art and architecture as well: a. Athama rules b. Shilpa Shastras c. Vastu Shastras

claims.text: The GI journal describes Mahabalipuram Stone Sculpture as having a wide forehead, sharp nose, long eyes, hanging ears and an oval face, usually with double chins.

quotes.quote: The Mahabalipuram Stone Sculpture is characterised by a wide forehead, sharp nose, long eyes, hanging ears and the oval shaped face, usually with double chins.

claims.text: The Konark stone carving GI application lists soft green serpentine from Kenthumundi, granite from Moyurbanj for heavy work, sandstone or saan patar for big cheap sculpture, and soft red naali stone.

quotes.quote: Soft green stone (Serpentine): lnitially it is looks like solid gray in color but when artisan work on it or wash the stone it become translucent green.
lt is very good in look. lt is got from the kenthumundi.
Granite: lt is used for heavy work. lt is dark and heaw stone got from the Moyurbanj.
Sand stone(Saan patar): it is used for rough big cheap sculpture.
Soft red stone (Naali stone): lt is very good at work. lt has fine lines and no translucency.

claims.text: The Konark application describes serpentine as soft compared with other dark rocks and often rich in metal ores, including chromium, manganese, cobalt and nickel.

quotes.quote: Compared to other dark rocks, serpentine is soft.
it is also often rich in other metal ores, including chromium, manganese, cobalt and nickel

claims.text: The Konark application calls its raw material the craft's most important feature, saying it uses serpentine, named for markings like snake skin, which other craftsmen do not employ.

quotes.quote: The most important feature of Konark stone carving is the raw material. Konark stone carving utilizes serpentine stone, which is not employed by other craftsmen. The stone is called serpentine because of its color and markings resembling the skin of snakes.

claims.text: The Konark application says car patch adhesive fixes and dries within 15 minutes, while Araldite takes 12 to 24 hours to join stone but bonds strongly.

quotes.quote: Car patch (Adhesive): lt is very much used in stone carving because of it's quick bond behavior (lt will fix and dry Wth in 15 min.).
Araldite (adhesive): lt is also used for joining the stone but it is takes long time to join (12 to 24 ours).Araldite is used because of its strong bonding.

claims.text: The Konark application's method breaks the block into main planes, drills the surface to depth, makes a rough outline, adds intricate work, removes tool marks with flat chisels and finishes every surface.

quotes.quote: The block of stone is broken down in to main planes or areas, following form of the desired shape.
Surface is drilled to various desired depths and unwanted material removed.
Main rough body outline is made. lntricate work is then made. Tool marks are removed with flat chisels.
Finally, all surfaces are meticulously finished.

claims.text: The Konark stone carving GI application says the work is confined to people of the Pathurias caste, with surnames such as Das, Mistri, Nayak and Maharana.

quotes.quote: The work is confined to people of Pathurias caste with surnames of Das, Mistri, Nayak, Maharana, etc.

claims.text: The Konark application names Konark in Puri district and nearby areas, and Bhubaneswar and its outskirts, as the main areas producing Konark stone carving.

quotes.quote: The main geographical areas of peroduction of konark stone carving are Konark ( district Puri , Orissa, India) and near-by areas and Bhubaneswar (Orissa, India) and its outskirts

claims.text: The Konark application gives Oriya names for carving tools, such as tagi for the chisel, gunati for a double-sided chisel, thuk thuka for a wooden hammer and mugura for a heavy one.

quotes.quote: known by special local names given in Oriya areTagi (chisel) Gunati(double sided chisel) Thuk thuka (wooden hammer) Mugura (heaw wooden hammer)

claims.text: The Konark stone carving GI application dates the art to the late 6th or early 7th century AD.

quotes.quote: The art dates back to the late 6h century or early 7th century AD

claims.text: NABARD's GI page says Mahoba's Gaura stone is a brilliant white stone of soft texture, found only in Gaurahari village and divided into parts for decorative crafts.

quotes.quote: Mahoba's excellent Gaura stone artistry is well-known throughout the country.

The brilliant white stone used in Gaura stonecraft is primarily found in this area. Owing to the soft texture of Gaura stone, it is divided into many parts, which are subsequently utilized to create a variety of decorative crafts.
Found only in the Gaurahari village, Gaura pathar is a bright natural stone.

claims.text: NABARD's page says Gaura stone is shaped with hammers and a chisel, chemically treated and left in boiling water overnight before carving, and finally polished with sand or carborundum.

quotes.quote: Using hammers and a chisel, the stone is meticulously shaped. It is then chemically treated and left in boiling water for a whole night before being carved.
Sand or particles of carborundum are used for polishing as the last finishing touch.

claims.text: After Rajasthan introduced its pneumoconiosis policy in 2019, 23,436 of 192,143 people screened were diagnosed with silicosis, a prevalence of 12% among stone carving and stone mining workers.

quotes.quote: The introduction of the pneumoconiosis policy in 2019 in Rajasthan led to the diagnosis of 23,436 cases of silicosis out of 192,143 persons screened, indicating a prevalence of 12% among stone carving and stone mining workers

claims.text: Rupani reports that investigators' studies in Rajasthan found silicosis more prevalent among stone carving workers than among stone mining workers.

quotes.quote: The investigators emphasized that their studies in Rajasthan revealed a higher prevalence of silicosis among stone carving workers compared to stone mining workers

quotes.quote: Around 50,000 workers are working in the agate industry in Khambhat, Gujarat

lede.text: Indian stone craft turns natural stones such as marble, sandstone, soapstone and granite into sculptures, idols, vases, lamps, tabletops and jali panels.

Stone carvers, known by the Sanskrit name shilpi, make statues of deities at centres such as Mamallapuram and in Odisha, the Shilpa Shastras set rules of proportion, posture and iconography for them, and many Indian craftsmen belong to the Viswakarma caste group of hereditary art and craft occupations.

Stone inlay, one of Agra's two stone craft traditions, cuts, polishes and inlays precious and semi-precious stones, generally in hard stone such as marble, as parchin kari, the Mughal adaptation of pietra dura.

Other stone work includes stone bead making and the cutting, grinding and polishing of agate at Khambhat, soft stone cutwork at Varanasi, Gaura stone craft at Mahoba and shajar stone jewellery at Banda.
