sentences.text: Granite is an igneous rock and marble a metamorphic rock but a hard stone, while soft stones, often called soapstones because some contain talc, are easier to carve than granite and easy to carve by hand, and vary in hardness, some very soft ones breaking easily.

Stone carving is practised all over India, the stones carved reflect regional variation in which stones are available, and in most places local varieties are mostly used owing to lower transport costs.

Sivonen describes four classes of stone carvers, from the master carver and design architect sthapati to the builders, plasterers and painters called vardhakin, categories that primarily reflect temple construction.

In Odisha, carvers from Puri, Bhubaneswar, Lalitagiri and Khiching carve deities and the Konark wheel, and a 2010-2011 study counted approximately 450 active soapstone craftsmen at Dhakotha, out of approximately 500, around 400 carving and approximately 50 turning.
The Konark stone carving GI application says the work is confined to people of the Pathurias caste and names Konark in Puri district, and Bhubaneswar, as its main areas of production.
Hundreds of carvers in Mamallapuram, one of the stone carving centres of India, mainly make sculptures of Hindu gods and goddesses.

Kenoyer, Vidale and Bhan described Khambhat, at the time they wrote, as one of the largest stone bead working centres of the world, and Possehl described its lapidary products reaching a market on four continents.
The Varanasi soft stone statement of case says stone working is no longer restricted to temple carvings and deities but also makes carved panels, tiles, paper weights and pen stands.

Possehl wrote that beadmaking in the Cambay area of Gujarat seems to have started as early as the third millennium BC with the Harappan settlement at Lothal, dated to about 2400 to 1700 BC, whose beads were shipped as far as Mesopotamia.
Harappan beads were chipped, ground and perforated with stone drills propelled by a bow, and Possehl found the same sequence of steps still used in Cambay.

UNESCO's summary dates the rock-cut sanctuaries of Mahabalipuram to the Pallava kings of the 7th and 8th centuries, its statement of value speaks of craftsmanship of the 6th century CE, and their influence spread to Cambodia, Annam and Java.

The Khajuraho temples in Madhya Pradesh were built in sandstone during the Chandella dynasty, which reached its apogee between 950 and 1050, and the 13th-century Sun Temple at Konark, the culmination of Kalingan temple architecture, represents the chariot of Surya.

UNESCO's summary says the white marble Taj Mahal was built between 1631 and 1648, its statement of value gives 1632 as the start, and its stone-cutters, inlayers and carvers were requisitioned from the whole empire and from Central Asia and Iran.

Shah Jahan was a strong proponent of pietra dura, adapted to the Mughal style as parchin kari, literally driven in, and sources differ on when inlay arrived: Dastkari Haat Samiti and Outlook Traveller credit Shah Jahan in the 17th century, while Live History India credits Humayun, citing a mosque of 1540 CE, and Dastkari Haat Samiti says Shah Jahan brought skilled Persian artisans to train local craftsmen.

Sources differ on when the Shilpa Shastras date from: Impart puts the texts generally in the early centuries of the second millennium CE, while Sivonen says they are contained principally in the Citralakshana and the Citrasutra, believed to date to the 5th century CE, and scholars question how far their rules were followed.

Sivonen found that Mamallapuram's carving industry developed to its present state through the sculpture college started in 1957 and the town's growth as a tourist destination, while the GI application says the Pallava techniques are still practised by its present sculptors.

Granite, an igneous rock, remains the main material for religious Hindu carvings in Tamil Nadu, and the Mahabalipuram GI application says its sculpture is made of pure granite, while Sivonen found the black granite of Mamallapuram sculpture was mostly blue metal, a slightly softer version of granite, 25 per cent basalt.

The Varanasi statement of case calls soapstone the softest form of limestone and its soft stone pyrophyllite, while Sivonen and Jha tie soapstone to talc, which Jha says makes it soft and craft-friendly.

Gadapa stone, also called durgi stone, a plain grey soft stone quarried in Andhra Pradesh, was the cheapest and softest stone carved in Mamallapuram, where marble had replaced it as the most popular stone for souvenirs during Sivonen's fieldwork.
The Konark sculptures are carved in khondalite, called Kanda pathar in Oriya, with laterite in the foundations and green chlorite for cult icons and occasionally door frames.

The Konark stone carving GI application lists soft green serpentine, which it calls the craft's most important feature, granite for heavy work, sandstone for big cheap sculpture and soft red naali stone.
The three Hoysala temples at Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura are built with chloritic schist.

Makrana marble from Rajasthan, the stone of the Taj Mahal's main mausoleum, was the first Global Heritage Stone Resource from India and from Asia, and the Taj's inlay uses semi-precious stones such as lapis lazuli, agate, carnelian and jade.

NABARD's GI pages describe Mahoba's Gaura stone as a brilliant white stone of soft texture found only in Gaurahari village, and Bhedaghat's stone crafts in Jabalpur as made from soft marble found on the banks of the Narmada.
Granite deposits are abundant in South India, so many temples and sculptures there have been made of granite throughout the centuries.
The beads of Gujarat have mostly been made from stone of the agate beds along the Narmada River, eroded over millennia from the basalt of the Deccan Trap and concentrated into workable beds.
The term khondalite, from the Kond tribe of Odisha, was coined by T. L. Walker in 1902 for rocks of quartz, felspar, garnet and sillimanite.
Khondalite was chosen at Konark for its availability nearby and its ease of sculpting over laterite, and the exact source of the stone and how it was carried are yet to be deciphered.

Mohapatra reports green chlorite, locally muguni, at Konark and notes Ganguly's 1912 view that the dark green rock is serpentinous or hornblendic rather than chlorite, while an EPCH report gives Mugunipathara as black granite.
Banda's district administration says shajar stone, also called fungus augite or tree augite, is found only in the Ken River.
In Mamallapuram, carving started with rough cutting the stone to size, drawing the statue on the block and cutting off the extra stone, and the whole statue was usually worked layer by layer.

In Mamallapuram, granite carvings were made mainly with electric tools introduced in the 1990s and soft stone carvings primarily by hand, and the Varanasi statement of case says unwanted material is chiselled out of harder stones and scraped out of softer ones with a sharp flat-edged iron tool.

The Konark stone carving GI application describes breaking the block into main planes, drilling the surface to depth, making a rough outline, adding intricate work, removing tool marks with flat chisels and finishing every surface.

Dhakotha carvers turn their pencil lines into surface-etched lines with a fine-tipped chisel and finish with sandpaper, and in Patthar Kundo turning two craftsmen work a handmade wooden lathe, one pulling a rope while the other carves.

In Cambay, agate bead blanks are chipped with a water buffalo horn hammer, ground on electric abrasive wheels, perforated with a bow-driven diamond-tipped bit and polished in drums of abrasive slurry for approximately a week.

For inlay, Outlook Traveller describes stones cut and shaped on a hand-operated machine and the marble chiselled with a diamond-tipped chisel, and the stones are set into the carved-out marble with an adhesive and polished.
The UP MSME portal describes Banda's shazar stones mounted on a wooden khunta stand and cut with silicon carbide powder, using a wooden bow with a delicate steel wire called kaman.

The Shilpa Shastras ask a sculptor to pay respect to the stone and his tools before work, and by them the eyes of a temple deity are carved only in its eye-opening ceremony, with a golden needle chisel.

Sivonen describes granite in Tamil Nadu being classed masculine, feminine or neutral by its sound when struck, and in Karnataka a Hoysala sculptor is taught to identify stones by their sound, male stones being used for gods, female stones for goddesses and neutral stones for objects.

Masculine ansila granite makes a clear, bell-like sound and is considered the best quality of stone, with the fewest cracks, while neutral nabunsagar is most prone to cracking and makes a drum-like sound.
Sivonen adds that such factors are considered general characteristics of Hindu stone carving but mainly show the ideals behind the work.
Heating raw agate in small pots of smouldering sawdust causes a physical change in the stone that makes chipping easier.
Soapstone is nonporous, nonabsorbent, heat resistant, of high specific heat capacity and resistant to acids and alkalis.

The Varanasi statement of case says carvers sprinkle water on the stone because friction from constant chiselling heats the tools, and a Mamallapuram carver controlled the carving through the angle of the chisel and the force of the hammer.

The khondalite of Konark weathers as its feldspars and red almandine garnet alter to kaolinite and goethite, its feldspar bands conspicuously kaolinitised and its garnet crystals dislodged, disfiguring the sculptures.
Mohapatra writes that Konark's structures of chloritised or serpentinised mafic rock are better preserved and not prone to weathering or grain decay.
Mohapatra describes laterite as a porous, pitted, clay-like rock formed by in situ alteration in tropical climates, with a hard limonitic crust holding much iron oxide and some aluminium oxide.
The Konark stone carving GI application describes serpentine as soft compared with other dark rocks and often rich in metal ores, including chromium, manganese, cobalt and nickel.
The Konark application says car patch adhesive fixes and dries within 15 minutes, while Araldite takes 12 to 24 hours to join stone but bonds strongly.

The Varanasi statement of case says the stone is kept in boiling water overnight and treated chemically before carving, which smoothens and whitens its surface, and NABARD's page says Gaura stone is chemically treated and left in boiling water overnight before carving.

Agate is ground on emery wheels that raise dust with fine particles of 2-5 micron reaching the alveoli, inhaled silica dust induces silicosis, and long-term exposure raises susceptibility to tuberculosis and the risk of lung cancer.

Chaudhury and colleagues cite earlier studies reporting that about 38% of workers in India's agate stone polishing industries develop silicosis in their lifetime, and that families living in the area develop it at 6.8 - 11.8 %.
Studies cited by Aggarwal and by Chaudhury and colleagues found respirable dust in household agate units about 15-fold higher than the permissible level, with more than 60% free silica.
Of 82 Khambhat agate workers interviewed in 2010 to 2011, 80% knew of dust-preventive methods such as wet grinding and cloth masks, but only 22% used them.

Of 53 chest-symptomatic agate workers enrolled at Shakarpur in 2007 and followed for 30 months, thirteen died in less than 3 years, aged 28 to 60, and tuberculosis and nutritional status strongly influenced mortality.

After Rajasthan introduced its pneumoconiosis policy in 2019, 23,436 of 192,143 people screened were diagnosed with silicosis, a prevalence of 12% among stone carving and stone mining workers, and studies there found silicosis more prevalent among stone carving workers than among miners.
At Mamallapuram, stone dust was the biggest problem, carvers used very little protective equipment, and many suffered eye and respiratory problems.

With no official record, some estimates put Mamallapuram's workshops at over 200, Sivonen counted 162 stone carving units there in September 2010, and salaried granite workers earned on average 300 rupees a day in 2010.
Indians were the main buyers of Mamallapuram's granite carvings, while foreign tourists also bought its soft stone statues as souvenirs.
In 2010, granite for Mamallapuram carving cost around 40,000 rupees per cubic metre against 10,000 rupees for blue metal, and gadapa stone cost around 150-250 rupees per square foot.

Chauhan wrote in 2023 that the Taj Mahal's floral ornamentation has inspired an industry of marble souvenirs inlaid with stones, synonymous with the crafts of Agra, and Dastkari Haat Samiti's account says Agra's marble inlay table tops as large as 6 x 4 feet are sold in India's major metros and exported.
Possehl reported that the Narmada agate mines were owned by the Government of India and leased by Siddi miners, and that in Cambay men did all the chipping while men and women ground the beads.

Women were 57% of the Khambhat agate workers surveyed in 2010 to 2011, Rupani's 2023 review says around 50,000 workers work in Khambhat's agate industry, and Chaudhury and colleagues wrote that Shakarpur's unorganized labourers had made agate ornaments for several decades.
EPCH's 2024 report says a customs notification effective from 30 October 2023 set a new duty drawback rate of 2.2% for stone artware and handicrafts.
Banda, a district of Uttar Pradesh, has shajar stone as its ODOP product, used mainly for making jewellery.
The rathas of Mahabalipuram are five monolithic temples, each hewn out of a huge boulder.
The Konark temple has 24 carved wheels, each about 3 m in diameter, and UNESCO's texts give its chariot six horses in one place and seven in another.
All surfaces of the Khajuraho temples are profusely carved, and Hoysala stone carvings cover the entire exterior surface of their temples.

The Shilpa texts require every sculpted image to have beauty, auspiciousness and verisimilitude, and the Vishnudharmottara Purana measures images in angulas, talas and mukhas, nine mukhas to a figure.
The GI journal describes Mahabalipuram Stone Sculpture as having a wide forehead, sharp nose, long eyes, hanging ears and an oval face, usually with double chins.
The relief work in marble and the inlay of precious and semi-precious stones make the Taj Mahal a monument apart, and Ebba Koch says its flowers symbolised the flora of Paradise.
Agra's stone artisans carve fret-work called jaali and carve within a carved object, a technique called undercut, mostly staying within the geometric and floral vocabulary of their forebears.
Dhakotha carvers make statues of Hindu gods and goddesses and architectural, decorative and household products, while its Patthar Kundo craft makes utensils.
Uttar Pradesh's MSME department names Rajasthan as famous for marble carving and Odisha for soapstone idols.
EPCH's 2024 report lists stone carving in marble, red and white stone among the crafts of the Jaipur, Alwar, Ajmer, Karoli and Dhaulpur clusters of Rajasthan, and yellow stone carving at Jaisalmer.
Several soapstone mines around Dhakotha in Kendujhar district keep its craft cluster self-dependent for raw material.
Cambay's lapidaries use stone from across India and neighbouring countries, and the inlaid stones of the Taj Mahal were procured from places as far off as Ceylon, China, Turkey, Tibet and Russia.
The Varanasi statement of case names Ramnagar in Varanasi district, Luxa, Mishir Pokhra and Lahartara among the areas of soft stone cutwork.
UNESCO names a Hassan District Committee for the Hoysala temples at Belur and Halebidu and a Mysuru District Committee for the Keshava Temple at Somanathapura.
